Readings / The payment arrived. What happened next?
Reading

When a cash transfer is paid into an account, what would show that the account became part of the recipient’s financial life?

The payment arrived. What happened next?

Report an error

Material on Yemen’s digital-payment pilot describes transfers paid into fully functional accounts, with recipient choice, for 45,460 recipients. That is an important step in delivery. It is not yet evidence that the accounts stayed part of recipients’ financial lives after the payments.

Evidence periodWorld Bank and G2Px material, May 2024 · reference period of the recipient figure not recorded · Cash Consortium of Yemen study (2026) and report (May 2026) and World Bank project documents (2025–2026) · UNICEF press releases (October and December 2024) · Cash Consortium of Yemen survey of January 2024 (posted online November 2024)
Last reviewed11 October 2026

What not to conclude

A delivered payment, a recipient count or an opened account is not durable active use unless follow-up shows continued use, and immediate cash-out is not by itself evidence of failure.

A transfer can succeed before a financial relationship begins. The intended recipient can be identified, the payment authorised and the funds delivered; the recipient can reach them; an account can be opened and made usable; and a programme can extend a new delivery channel into places where distributing cash is hard. Those are real results, and they should be measured and credited as such. Financial inclusion asks a different question: what happens after the money arrives?

World Bank and G2Px material from May 2024 describes a digital-payment pilot in eight districts within Yemen’s unconditional cash-transfer programme, reported by programme partners to have benefited 45,460 recipients. The pilot emphasised payment into fully functional accounts and recipient choice. That goes beyond a change in disbursement technology. A fully functional account can, by design, receive money, hold value and make payments; and choice matters because a system built around recipients should not treat them as passive receivers of a programme payment.

But possibility is not persistence. The available Yemen evidence does not yet tell us whether recipients used those accounts between transfers, kept balances in them, received other money, paid merchants or bills, made transfers of their own, switched providers, or kept using the account after the programme payments that prompted it weakened or ended. That is the missing observation.

Delivery and inclusion are different results

A digital cash-transfer programme may improve delivery even if recipients later withdraw most or all of each transfer in cash. Immediate cash-out can be rational: local merchants may prefer cash, acceptance networks may be thin, liquidity may be uncertain, and fees, distance, reliability, trust or familiarity may make cash the better instrument for immediate needs. Cash-out should not automatically be labelled failure, and account opening should not automatically be labelled inclusion.

Two Cash Consortium of Yemen studies of recipients of the Consortium partners' humanitarian cash assistance, a programme separate from the unconditional cash transfer, in sub-districts that the studies place in areas under the internationally recognized government, point to debt repayment as a common use of transfers. In a survey of recipient households in Ad-Dali and Ja’ar in January 2024 (291 and 209 interviews), posted online by its host in November 2024, 40% reported debt repayment among their regular expenses in the 30 days before the interview: about 47% of households that had received a transfer in those 30 days and about 30% of those that had not. In a 2026 study comparing three and six monthly transfers in Ja’ar, “debts are paid off” was one of the two most common answers to which part of the household economy improved most at the endline in November 2025 (one answer allowed): 60% of the 45 households that received six transfers gave it, and 40% of the 107 that received three. In the 2024 study, 11 of 21 business owners who answered in Ad-Dali and 10 of 21 in Ja’ar said that fewer customers bought on credit when cash assistance was distributed. These are local samples of aid recipients and business owners, not national estimates, and the business owners' answers are counts of interviews, not credit volumes. They are one reason why immediate cash-out is not, by itself, a sign that a transfer failed.

It is more useful to report three families of results separately:

  • Delivery: was the right payment made to the right person, safely, accurately and on time?
  • Access to a usable account: did the recipient obtain a genuinely functional account, on terms they could understand, with a meaningful choice?
  • Persistent use: did the account keep a role in the recipient’s financial life between or after programme payments?

Each can improve while another remains unmeasured.

The period between payments may tell us most

A payment-day metric tells us whether the programme worked on payment day. Persistence runs on another clock. Useful questions include:

  • Was the account still active a month, three months, six months and a year later?
  • Was it used between transfer cycles?
  • Did money from outside the programme enter the account?
  • Was some value kept rather than withdrawn at once?
  • Did the recipient pay a merchant or a bill from it, or start a transfer?
  • Was it used after the programme payments ended?
  • Did the recipient stay with the provider, switch or stop?
  • What happened when a transaction failed or a complaint was made?
  • What did using the account cost in money, time and travel?

The aim is not to expect every cash-transfer recipient to become a frequent user of digital finance. It is to find out whether the new channel created an option of lasting value, and for whom.

Choice matters only if it can be exercised

The pilot’s emphasis on recipient choice is analytically important. Whether an account can become more than a payment channel depends on design features such as a real choice of provider, a fully functional account, reachable access points, clear terms and the ability to use the account beyond the programme payment.

But choice written into a programme design is not necessarily choice experienced by recipients. Exercising it needs viable providers or channels, understandable fees, usable access points, control of credentials, reliable service and a practical ability to switch. So the measurement question is not only whether choice was offered, but whether recipients could exercise it without risking their access to the payment.

The pilot sat inside a much larger programme. UNICEF, which implemented the World Bank-funded unconditional cash transfer programme with the Social Fund for Development, announced in October 2024 that more than 1.43 million families were receiving assistance in its 18th payment cycle, which ran to mid-October, at payment sites, through mobile teams and home outreach, and in an e-wallet pilot; the figure is the cycle's announced reach, not a count of confirmed payments. In December 2024 it announced that the 19th cycle, starting on 11 December 2024 at fixed payment sites, marked the end of the programme in its then-current form. The pilot's 45,460 recipients and the programme's 1.43 million families are different counts, and one is not a share of the other; a family reached by a payment cycle does not thereby hold an account.

Where the evidence stops

The current evidence does not establish that Yemen’s pilot produced persistent use. It does not establish that cashing out was irrational or undesirable, or that paying transfers digitally automatically improves household resilience, women’s agency or financial health. And it does not establish that the pilot failed simply because those later outcomes have not been measured. The 45,460 figure counts recipients reported by the programme, not people who kept using an account.

The appraisal document of the World Bank-financed FMIIP project (May 2025) reports a separate count from a pilot, without saying whether it is the pilot described above: by the end of payment cycle 18 (16 September–17 October 2024), 10,761 wallets had been opened with cash transfers paid into them, and take-up ranged from 40% to 70% across pilot districts. The two documents differ in date and unit, and may not describe the same pilot — recipients reported in May 2024, wallets opened by October 2024 — so no ratio between 10,761 and 45,460 is published or implied.

The programme has run no payment cycle since January 2025, for lack of funds, according to the World Bank's implementation report on ESPECRP, the emergency social protection project that finances it, archived on 30 June 2026; the project is due to close on 31 December 2026. The Cash for Nutrition and Livelihoods Project, approved on 30 June 2026 and with a financing agreement signed on 2 September 2026, builds on ESPECRP's delivery systems but is designed to pay a different benefit, six months of cash for nutrition to pregnant women and mothers of children under two; it does not restore the unconditional transfers.

Three later findings mark where the evidence stops. A Cash Consortium of Yemen study (2026) compared three and six monthly transfers using programme data, with no randomised design and no group of households without assistance: households on six transfers showed modest further gains in food security and less negative coping than those on three, and savings could not be compared, because only three households, all of them on six transfers, reported putting any money aside. And the appraisal document of the Cash for Nutrition and Livelihoods Project (June 2026) reports from the programme's monitoring that “high transaction costs and long distances to financial service points severely impeded e-wallet uptake”, and sets out a plan for recipients to cash out through agents hired by financial service providers, given the scarcity of bank branches and ATMs. The third, a separate May 2026 report by the Cash Consortium of Yemen based on desk research, a small survey of traders in Taiz and interviews with a few financial and humanitarian experts, concerns access to cash itself: it reports that in areas administered by the internationally recognized government, currency exchangers and banks limited currency exchange and the rials they handed out from February 2026, and rial withdrawals from late April; its summary gives the period as late February to mid-May, and it does not report the limits ending. That is reported practice in those areas and months, not a measure of how many people were affected, and the report attributes it to the regional conflict and to cash hoarding without testing that explanation.

The same May 2026 report adds an observation on cash-out. It says that most multi-purpose cash assistance (MPCA: the humanitarian cash programmes the report covers, not the unconditional cash transfer, which has run no payment cycle since January 2025) was disbursed through microfinance banks as vouchers that recipients exchange at local agents of financial service providers and, citing one interview with an MPCA programme manager in April 2026, that during the Ramadan and Eid holiday period agents often lacked enough cash, with waits of four to five hours. It reports that funds were released only in denominations of YER 100 and 200 and, citing the same interview, that an e-wallet pilot disbursed funds without problems or delays. These are reported observations, some of them from a single interview. The paragraph names no programme or area, though the report frames the liquidity crisis as affecting areas under the internationally recognized government, rural recipients most, and says that liquidity problems for MPCA programmes eased after the period of high demand. The e-wallet result concerns disbursement, not whether recipients could then obtain cash, which the report itself calls unclear.

The pilot material provides evidence of movement toward digital delivery and describes recipients being given usable accounts. Whether that became a durable financial relationship is a separate empirical question.

Before counting a payment as inclusion

Before counting a programme payment as financial inclusion, check which result the figure measures: delivery, access to a usable account, or persistent use. A recipient count, an opened wallet or a take-up rate is not continued use, and immediate cash-out is not, by itself, a failure. Check the date and unit of each pilot figure before setting two of them side by side, and whether the programme was still paying in the period described.

What would change this reading?

A longitudinal follow-up of recipients, linked where appropriate and safely possible to administrative payment data. At minimum it would distinguish payment success, account activation, the timing of cash-out, activity between transfers, activity a month, three months, six months and a year later, balances kept, deposits from outside the programme, payments and transfers the recipient starts, switching provider, dormancy, complaints, failed or reversed transactions, fees, the cost in travel and time, control of the account, and use after the transfers end. It should then ask recipients why they used, returned, switched or stopped.

If the account disappears from the recipient’s financial life between one payment and the next, did digitisation change the delivery channel, or did it change the financial relationship?

Related measurement priorities

Each priority below would supply evidence that this Reading says is missing; the link does not mean the priority would settle the Reading.

Measurement priorityP0 · Social protection / Payments
Persistence of financial use after cash transfers
Programme evidence can establish delivery, beneficiary reach, successful payout and exposure to an account or wallet; sustained use after the transfer remains unmeasured. An existing instrument records respondents in both areas of control: the World Bank's mobile phone survey of August–September 2022 records each respondent's area of control and asks respondents to rank their three most important sources of income; a later round could add questions on how transfers are received and used. UNICEF's releases on the World Bank-funded unconditional cash transfer give its announced reach, not confirmed payments, and its channels in the 18th payment cycle, to mid-October 2024 (payment sites, mobile teams and home outreach, and an e-wallet pilot), and announce that the 19th cycle, from 11 December 2024, would end the programme in its then-current form. A May 2026 report on humanitarian multi-purpose cash assistance, a different programme, records from one interview agents short of cash at cash-out during the Ramadan and Eid holiday period.
Evidence needed: Longitudinal programme or provider cohort data, or repeated beneficiary follow-up, with privacy-safe linkage from transfer receipt to account or wallet activation, repeat use, merchant use, saving and cash-out.
Decision it would strengthen: This evidence would show whether transfer-related financial exposure becomes persistent use and which observed conditions are associated with repeat use.

Related readings

Evidence periodProvider data 2016–2019, from a 2020 study of five e-money providers · CBY-Aden payment reports 2024–2025 and the FMIIP baseline of January 2025, shown beside the historical data, not as a continuation
When does digital growth become durable use?
Historical evidence from Yemen records a large base of e-money accounts by 2019 alongside dormancy, one-off use and a transaction mix still closely tied to cash. The open question is whether people choose to return to digital finance and find enough value to keep using it.
Evidence periodPoint-of-sale (POS) counts March 2025 – June 2026 · institutional records June–August 2026 · project results framework January 2025
When does a payment reform become financial inclusion?
A rule can be issued, infrastructure can expand, institutions can be created and transactions can appear while evidence on reach, repeated use, service quality, protection and outcomes remains incomplete. The question is how far a reform’s effects can actually be traced.
